1:
Clarke opens by demolishing the title. The versions offer four different headings — a memorial to Israel, "a commemoration concerning the Sabbath", a thanksgiving and prophecy, and a note attaching the psalm to David's rejection by Achish — and he dismisses them together: "never was a title more misplaced or less expressive of the contents. There is no mention of the Sabbath in it; there is no thanksgiving in it, for it is deeply penitential."

Augustine builds his whole exposition on the heading Clarke rejects. "What is this Sabbath?... The Sabbath is rest. Doubtless he was in some disquietude, who with groaning was calling the Sabbath to remembrance." The misery is therefore the blessing: "happy he who is wretched after this manner!" — for "he would be miserable, if he were not a mourner." He also parts the psalm's two verbs: "not all who are rebuked will be chastened", some being "saved in the chastening" though "so as by fire", while others "will not be corrected."

Calvin and Henry take the remembering seriously without the Sabbath. Calvin rejects the theory that the title names a tune as "unnatural, and without foundation", reading it as David's memorial to himself, "lest he should too soon forget the chastisement by which God had afflicted him", and to others, since as "master and teacher over the whole Church" what he learned had to be made known.

On the occasion Delitzsch and Clarke agree and both hedge. Delitzsch treats David's adultery as the likely cause, which would set the psalm in a chronological series with three others, and describes the sufferer as "distressed both in mind and body, forsaken by his friends, and regarded by his foes as one who is cast off for ever." Clarke calls the same occasion "the most likely", but "of what nature we are left to conjecture."

The arrows are read at every level. Clarke keeps them physical, "the acute pains which he endured; each appearing to his feeling as if an arrow were shot into his body". Wesley splits them, "thy judgments outward and inward"; Henry makes them "the terrors of God", which "are sure to stick where they hit". Spurgeon prefers the spiritual sense as the sharper, and finds a mercy in the aim: God "shoots at their sins rather than them, and those who feel his sin-killing shafts in this life, shall not be slain with his hot thunderbolts in the next world." Ellicott refuses to draw any conclusion from the figure, since the same image serves for disease, for famine, and for divine judgments generally, so that "by itself it therefore decides nothing as to the particular cause of the Psalmist's grief"; he retranslates it "thine arrows have fallen deep into me, And fallen upon me has thine hand."

Whether the sores are real is the tile's sharpest division. Clarke will not allow the metaphor: "I do not see that we can understand the word in any figurative or metaphorical way. I believe they refer to some disease" — though "whether the leprosy, the small pox, or some other disorder cannot be absolutely determined." Ellicott supports him clinically, correcting "wounds" to "stripes" and noting that both following words "denote suppuration; the first in reference to the offensive smell, the second of the discharge of matter." Gill takes the opposite course, making the wounds the psalmist's sins, for which "there is no healing but in a wounded Saviour". Wesley glosses the folly that caused them as "sin"; Ellicott remarks that "men are generally even more loth to confess their folly than their sins."

Ellicott retranslates the sixth verse as "I am made to writhe, I am bowed down exceedingly, All day long I go about squalid". Spurgeon petitions rather than describes: "chasten me if thou wilt, it is a Father's prerogative... but, O turn not the rod into a sword, smite not so as to kill."
7:
The loathsome disease is a burning, and all three philologists say so. Clarke corrects the English — "or rather, a burning", from a root meaning to fry or scorch, hence "a strongly feverish disease". Ellicott agrees the word means "inflamed or inflammation", while noting that the ancient versions derived it from a different root, "to be light, or made light of", and rendered it "mockings". Gill reports both senses; on the second, the psalmist "was vile in his own eyes."

Wesley states the rule the whole tile turns on. The disease "might be some burning fever, breaking forth outwardly in carbuncles, or boils"; and though "this and the other expressions may be taken figuratively", the principle is that "we should not forsake the literal sense of the words without necessity."

Clarke follows that rule and then stops short of using it. "That David describes a natural disease here cannot reasonably be doubted; but what that disease was, who shall attempt to say?" He declines a diagnosis he could give: "it would be easy to show a disease of which what he here enumerates are the very general symptoms; but I forbear, because in this I might attribute to one what would be more especially descriptive of another." Ellicott is content to retranslate — "I am become deadly cold, and am quite worn out" — and to note that the disquietness is "properly, roaring".

Where the psalmist turns to God the tone changes, and Delitzsch marks it precisely: having bewailed his suffering, "he goes on in a somewhat calmer tone: it is the calm of weariness, but also of the rescue which shows itself from afar. He has complained, but not as if it were necessary first of all to make God acquainted with his suffering." Ellicott catches the same movement as a reflex: "notice the clutch at the thought of divine justice, as the clutch of a drowning man amid that sea of trouble." Spurgeon draws the comfort out — the desire is "if unuttered, yet perceived", since "what we cannot tell to him he perfectly understands", and "the good Physician understands the symptoms of our disease and sees the hidden evil which they reveal": "none more lonely than the broken-hearted sinner, yet hath he the Lord for his companion."

The panting heart is heard in the Hebrew itself: Ellicott points out that the word, "like palpitate, expresses the beating of the heart, by its sound", and Clarke renders it "flutters, palpitates, through fear and alarm". Clarke takes the failing strength medically, as an inability "to take nourishment", and the lost light of the eyes as failing sight; Spurgeon takes both at once — "sweet light departed from his bodily eye, and consolation vanished from his soul" — and finds the cause of the palpitation in the desertion: "the soul seeks sympathy in sorrow, and if it finds none, its sorrowful heart-throbs are incessant."

Why the friends stand off is the tile's last question, and the answers differ in how much blame they assign. Gill offers a range: they feared infection, or "could not bear the stench of his wounds", or took the case for desperate; and though the law would have required distance had it been leprosy, "this rather seems to be voluntary, and to proceed from neglect and contempt." Clarke makes it theological rather than sanitary: "they considered me as suffering under a Divine judgment; and, thinking me an accursed being, they avoided me lest they should be infected by my disease." Ellicott agrees, and puts their reasoning in their own mouths: looking on him as "one smitten of God", thinking "he must be wicked to deserve such pain", they "abandon him as too vile for their society." He also sharpens the last word: the kinsmen are "rather neighbours, or near ones", so that the complaint is that "those who should have been near me stand aloof."
12:
Henry draws up a five-count indictment. The enemies are cruel, since "it is the blood of the saints that is thirsted after"; subtle, since "mischief, covered and carried on by deceit, may well be called a snare"; insolent, watching for the moment when the sufferer should "misplace a word, or take a false step"; ungrateful, so that "for my love they are my adversaries"; and impious, "my adversaries merely because I follow the thing that good is." Hence the general observation: such men "hate prayer even in those that pray for them, and hate peace even in those that would be at peace with them." Clarke lowers the charge — "perhaps this means only that they wished for his death" — while Wesley keeps the concealment: "they design mischief, but cover it with fair pretences."

Why the psalmist answers nothing is the tile's real question, and each voice gives a different reason. Clarke makes it guilt: "I was conscious of my guilt, I could not vindicate myself; and I was obliged in silence to bear their insults." Wesley makes it submission — the silence testifies "his humiliation for his sins, and his acceptation of the punishment which he had brought upon himself." Gill makes it imitation, the psalmist acting "the part of a deaf man" as Saul did under the sons of Belial and as Christ did before his accusers, bearing "all the railings and calumnies of men with calmness and patience"; at the next verse he supplies a fourth reason, that the calm came from hope.

Both grammarians hear a courtroom in the wording. Clarke calls the word for reproofs "arguments or vindications; a forensic term": "I was as a man accused in open court, and I could make no defense." Ellicott renders it "replies or justifications". Spurgeon supplies the consolation: "reputation like a fair pearl may be cast into the mire, but in due time... the godly character shall shine with unclouded splendour."

Clarke pauses over a textual point nobody else raises: the printed Hebrew has one divine name where over a hundred manuscripts have another, which he explains from the practice of never pronouncing the sacred name but substituting the other in reading. Ellicott notes only that the pronoun in the same clause is emphatic.

The prayer's motive is a fear of being laughed at, and Ellicott makes the syntax carry it, keeping the conditional force throughout: "For I said, Lest they should rejoice over me: Lest, when my foot slipped, they should vaunt themselves against me." Spurgeon feels the exposure keenly: "the least flaw in a saint is sure to be noticed; the merest trip of the foot sets all the dogs of hell barking." His conclusion is practical: "how careful ought we to be, and how importunate in prayer for upholding grace!"

Being "ready to halt" is read as weakness or as readiness. Clarke takes the first, literally: "I am prepared to halt. So completely infirm is my soul, that it is impossible for me to take one right step in the way of righteousness, unless strengthened by thee." Wesley glosses it "just falling into destruction", Spurgeon "one who limps, or a person with tottering footsteps". Gill offers both a proneness to sin and a liability to adversity, and takes the second in an unexpected direction: the psalmist was "prepared for it", having "considered that he was born for trouble and adversity", so that "when it came upon him it was no strange thing to him."

The confession that closes the movement is measured by its object. Clarke says only that he will confess "with the deepest humiliation and self-abasement"; Gill weighs whether the declaring is made to men or rather to God, "who only could pardon him". Ellicott supplies the test: "the note of true penitence is here. The sorrow is for the sin itself, not for its miserable results."
19:
Two of them would rewrite the nineteenth verse, and by the same amount. Clarke proposes to read "without cause" for "lively" — "a change made by the half of one letter" — and offers the result: "But without cause my enemies have strengthened themselves; and they who wrongfully hate me are multiplied. Here the one member of the verse answers to the other." Ellicott reaches the same suspicion independently, "the parallelism and a comparison with" a companion psalm pointing that way. Gill defends the received text by defining the life narrowly: the enemies are alive neither spiritually, having "no lively hope, nor living faith", nor merely naturally, but are "in great prosperity and worldly happiness". Wesley agrees in three words — they "are thriving and flourishing".

Clarke has no patience with the next verse's English: "the translation is as bad as the sentence is awkward", and the sense is simply "because I follow goodness". He then reports something stranger. Several versions carry an addition here that the Hebrew does not have — "they have rejected me, the beloved one, as an abominable dead carcass" — which he supposes the translator meant to apply to Christ, noting that the reading "was found in some Greek and Latin copies" of an earlier age. His conclusion is an open admission: "whence this reading came I cannot conjecture."

Delitzsch answers the question Clarke leaves open. He records the same interpolation across the Greek, Latin, Ethiopic, Syriac and Arabic texts, notes that an early father referred it to Absalom, and supplies the source: the words are lifted from Isaiah.

Where the psalm ends divides them more deeply than any reading. Delitzsch insists that it does not resolve: the poet "closes with sighs for help. No lighting up of the darkness of wrath takes place. The fides supplex is not changed into fides triumphans" — the only relief being the two words "O Lord, my salvation". Spurgeon hears those same two words as a completed victory: "not my Saviour only, but my salvation. He who has the Lord on his side has salvation in present possession." Faith "foresees the blessed issue of all her pleas", so that "a sense of sin shall melt into the joy of salvation; grief shall lead on to gratitude."

The prayer against desertion is read against the desertion already described. Gill notices the tense: the petition is that God "continue not to forsake", the psalmist seeming to have been "under divine desertion" already. Clarke sets the two abandonments side by side: "though all have forsaken me, do not thou"; "though my friends keep aloof, be thou near to help me." Spurgeon totals the losses — "when sickness, slander, and sin, all beset a saint, he requires the especial aid of heaven" — and asks for the one relation that survives: "let me feel that though friendless besides, I have a most gracious and all-sufficient friend in thee."

The haste is justified by the state of the man. Clarke reduces it to "I am dying; save, Lord, or I perish"; Gill notes that the case "required haste", and that God helps "when none else can". Spurgeon finds a use in the urgency itself: "see how sorrow quickens the importunity of prayer! Here is one of the sweet results of affliction" — and adds a promise about the accounting, that "in heaven we shall see that we had not one trial too many, or one pang too severe."

Clarke closes the psalm with a warning rather than a comfort. Whoever reads it through "will see what a grievous and bitter thing it is to sin against the Lord, and especially to sin after having known his mercy." The application is direct: "a life of righteousness may be lost by giving way to a moment's temptation, and a fair character sullied for ever!"
